content: 1. New technologies, such as eHealth systems and satellite imagery, are being utilized to enhance the performance and efficiency of health systems. 2. The environmental impact of the health sector is being evaluated, and mechanisms to monitor carbon emissions and other environmental effects are being developed. 3. Health facilities are prioritizing sustainability in the selection of products and procurement of services, including energy, water, transport, and waste management. 4. Climate change poses significant threats to health through environmental determinants, which are strongly influenced by social conditions. A Health in All Policies approach is being promoted to address these challenges. 5. Expanding multisectoral public health prevention programs can mitigate negative health outcomes at their source and enable timely, effective responses to evolving environmental and climate-related risks. 6. Policies and programs in sectors such as agriculture, transport, housing, and energy can reduce health risks and improve health practices, behaviors, and processes. 7. Although the health sector does not typically have direct control over environmental determinants, it plays a critical role in providing evidence, raising awareness, monitoring environmental exposures and outcomes, defining regulatory standards, and managing health risks. 8. Active coordination and intersectoral planning are essential for addressing environmental determinants of health. 9. Examples of joint actions between health ministries and other sectors include defining and monitoring air quality standards, promoting energy-efficient heating and cooking, and implementing health impact assessments for key transport programs. 10. Water resource management policies are integrating health considerations, including the implementation of climate-resilient water safety plans and monitoring water quality standards. 11. Food security forecasting, nutritional screening, and integrated vector management are being prioritized in collaboration with agriculture and food safety sectors. 12. Housing and infrastructure planning now account for flood and storm risks, with improved building designs, ventilation standards, and disaster management plans. 13. Waste management strategies emphasize minimization, safe disposal, and recycling, supported by municipal services. 14. Climate-informed health programming is increasingly incorporating climate risks and vulnerabilities into assessments, planning, and implementation to build resilience. 15. Health systems are adapting to address climate-sensitive health risks, such as vector-borne and waterborne diseases, extreme weather events, and nutritional crises. 16. Disaster risk reduction and public health preparedness efforts are being revised to ensure sustainability and effectiveness in the face of climate change. 17. Health programs are using climate data to identify capacity gaps, inform policy, and guide strategic investments and planning decisions. 18. Early warning systems for potential outbreaks or extreme weather events are enabling health programs to prepare for increased patient loads and special needs. 19. Emergency preparedness and management plans are being developed to address health risks associated with climate variability, emphasizing proactive measures over reactive responses. 20. Health infrastructure, including water supplies, drainage, waste disposal, telecommunications, energy supplies, and medical transport, is being designed to withstand extreme weather events. 21. Community-based actions are central to protecting health during emergencies, leveraging local knowledge of risks and vulnerabilities to address actual needs. 22. Empowered and well-organized communities can reduce risks, save lives, and minimize the impact of emergencies. 23. The World Health Organization (WHO) is developing an Emergency and Disaster Risk Management for Health (EDRM-H) Policy Framework to guide effective risk management. 24. Financial costs associated with protecting health from climate change are being assessed, including the need for expanded surveillance, retrofitting health facilities, and implementing climate-resilient water and food security measures. 25. Resource requirements, available finances, and funding gaps are being evaluated to mobilize and allocate resources effectively for climate and health challenges.
